ety.text: From Middle French vélocité, from Latin vēlōcitās (“speed”), from vēlōx (“fast”), thus a doublet of veloce.

senses.d: A vector quantity that denotes the rate of change of position with respect to time, combining speed with a directional component.
ex: A car racing in a circle may retain the same speed while continually changing its velocity.
The train was travelling at a slower velocity than usual.

senses.d: The number of times that an average unit of currency is spent during a specific period of time.
The value corresponding to how hard a key is struck on a MIDI controller or keyboard.

ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁-der. Latin vēlōx Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-ts Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts Proto-Italic *-tāts Latin -tās Latin vēlōcitātembor. Spanish velocidad Borrowed from Latin vēlōcitātem. By surface analysis, veloz + -idad.
Borrowed from Latin vēlōcitātem, corresponding to veloz + -idade.
From Old French vistece. By surface analysis, vite + -esse.

From Middle English velvet, velwet, veluet, from Old Occitan veluet, from Vulgar Latin *villutittus, diminutive of villūtus, from Latin villus (“shaggy hair, tuft of hair”). Cognate with French velours.

senses.d: A closely woven fabric (originally of silk, now also of cotton or man-made fibres) with a thick short pile on one side.
Very fine fur, including the skin and fur on a deer's antlers.
ex: His [a hart's] head when it commeth firſt out, hath a ruſſet pyll vpon it, the which is called Veluet, […]

senses.d: To cover with velvet or with a covering of a similar texture.
ex: Penmachno mill is situate where a stream has furrowed a deep channel, and velveted the rocks with the richest mosses […].
Last week the scaffolds were up in the hall once more. This time the back wall is to be velveted in absorbent fiber glass […]

senses.d: To coat raw meat in starch, then in oil, preparatory to frying.
To remove the velvet from a deer's antlers.

ex: She spoke very gently, full of compassion for the boy, velveting her reproach for me.

senses.d: Soft and delicate, like velvet; velvety.
Peaceful; carried out without violence; especially as pertaining to the peaceful breakup of Czechoslovakia.
ex: There is such a thing as a velvet divorce: if Canada or Belgium were to split apart, the consequences would be unfortunate but manageable.

ety.text: Inherited from Old French velor, an alteration of velos, either from velu (“hairy”) + -os (“-ous”), or a borrowing from Old Occitan velos; either way, from Latin villus. Cognate with English velvet and a doublet of villeux.
From Late Latin villūtus, derived from Latin villus (“hair, tuft”).

ety.text: Latin tertiusbor. Spanish tercioder. Proto-Indo-European *pil-? Latin pilus Spanish peloder. Spanish terciopelo From tercio (“third”) + pelo (“hair”).
Inherited from Late Latin villūtus. By surface analysis, vello + -udo.
Borrowed from Catalan vellut, from Late Latin villūtus, derived from Latin villus (“tuft, hair”).

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French duvet, from Old French duvet (“down, the feathers of young birds”), alteration of dumet, dumect, from Old French dum, dun (“down, feathers”), from Old Norse dúnn (“down, down feather”), from Proto-Germanic *dūnaz (“down”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“to smoke, fume, raise dust”).
